items.readable_text:
Content:
When the characteristic equation of a Cauchy-Euler equation has a repeated root [MATH: \lambda = c,] the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(x) = c_1 x^c + c_2 x^c \ln x.]

Content:
To illustrate, let's solve the following Cauchy-Euler equation:

Content:
[MATH: x^2y''-xy'+y=0]

Content:
Differentiating the trial solution [MATH: y = x^\lambda] with respect to [MATH: x] gives

Content:
[MATH: y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}.]

Content:
Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

Content:
[MATH: x^{2}λ(λ − 1)x^{λ − 2} − xλx^{λ − 1} + x^{λ}|= 0; λ(λ − 1)x^{λ} − λx^{λ} + x^{λ}|= 0; x^{λ}(λ(λ − 1) − λ + 1)|= 0.]

Content:
So, we have the following characteristic equation:

Content:
[MATH: λ(λ − 1) − λ + 1|= 0; λ^{2} − 2λ + 1|= 0; (λ − 1)^{2}|= 0]

Content:
The characteristic equation has a double root [MATH: \lambda = 1.] Therefore, the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: y(x)|= c_{1}x^{1} + c_{2}x^{1}\ln x; = c_{1}x + c_{2}x\ln x.]

sections.readable_text:
Find the general solution to the equation
[MATH: 2x^2 y'' + 6 xy' + 2y = 0, \qquad x>0.]

sections.normalized_html:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form [MATH: y=x^\lambda.] Differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: x] gives

[MATH: y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}.]

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

[MATH: 2x^{2} ⋅ λ(λ − 1)x^{λ − 2} + 6x ⋅ λx^{λ − 1} + 2x^{λ}|= 0; 2λ(λ − 1)x^{λ} + 6λx^{λ} + 2x^{λ}|= 0; x^{λ}[2λ(λ − 1) + 6λ + 2]|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

[MATH: 2λ(λ − 1) + 6λ + 2|= 0; 2λ^{2} + 4λ + 2|= 0; 2(λ^{2} + 2λ + 1)|= 0; 2(λ + 1)^{2}|= 0]

The characteristic equation has a double root [MATH: \lambda = -1.] Therefore, the general solution is [MATH: y(x)|= c_{1}x^{− 1} + c_{2}x^{− 1}\ln x; = (c_{1})/(x) + (c_{2}\ln x)/(x).]

[MATH: 2x^2 y'' + 6 xy' + 2y = 0, \qquad x>0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form [MATH: y=x^\lambda.] Differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: x] gives

[MATH: y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}.]

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

[MATH: 2x^{2} ⋅ λ(λ − 1)x^{λ − 2} + 6x ⋅ λx^{λ − 1} + 2x^{λ}|= 0; 2λ(λ − 1)x^{λ} + 6λx^{λ} + 2x^{λ}|= 0; x^{λ}[2λ(λ − 1) + 6λ + 2]|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

[MATH: 2λ(λ − 1) + 6λ + 2|= 0; 2λ^{2} + 4λ + 2|= 0; 2(λ^{2} + 2λ + 1)|= 0; 2(λ + 1)^{2}|= 0]

The characteristic equation has a double root [MATH: \lambda = -1.] Therefore, the general solution is
[MATH: y(x)|= c_{1}x^{− 1} + c_{2}x^{− 1}\ln x; = (c_{1})/(x) + (c_{2}\ln x)/(x).]

sections.normalized_html:

  • First, we apply the condition [MATH: y(1)=0.] Substituting [MATH: y(1)= 0] into the general solution gives [MATH: 0= c_1.]

  • Then, we apply the condition [MATH: y'(1) = 1.] Differentiating [MATH: y,] we get [MATH: y^{′}|= 10c_{1}x^{9} + c_{2}x^{9} + 10c_{2}x^{9}\ln x.]

Substituting [MATH: y'(1)=1] and [MATH: c_1 = 0] into the above gives [MATH: 1|= 10c_{1} + c_{2}; 1|= 0 + c_{2}; c_{2}|= 1.]

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is [MATH: y(x) = x ^{10}\ln x .]
